text: Solar system
Eight planets orbit the Sun. Mars is the fourth, 1.52 times farther out than Earth (1.52 AU), so it receives only 43% of Earth's sunlight. A Mars year lasts 687 Earth days (668.6 sols).

Kepler's third law: T² = a³, with T in years and a in AU. Mars' orbit is eccentric (e = 0.093), so sunlight at the top of its atmosphere varies from about 492 W/m² at aphelion to 717 W/m² at perihelion. That swing drives its seasons and global dust storms.

Planets

Rocky planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small and dense. Gas and ice giants (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are mostly hydrogen, helium and ices. Mars is 53% of Earth's diameter and has 11% of its mass.
Surface gravity g = GM/r². For Mars, M = 6.417 × 10²³ kg and r = 3,389.5 km, so g = 3.72 m/s² (0.38 g). Escape velocity √(2GM/r) is 5.03 km/s, against Earth's 11.19 km/s.
Moons

Mars has two small moons. Phobos (27 x 22 x 18 km) orbits only 6,000 km above the surface, three times a sol. Deimos (15 x 12 x 10 km) orbits farther out. Both may be captured asteroids or debris from an ancient impact.
Phobos orbits inside the synchronous altitude, so tides drag it inward by about 1.8 m per century. In 30 to 50 million years it will hit Mars or break up into a ring.
Stars
The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star with a surface temperature of about 5,772 K. A star's colour shows its temperature: cooler stars look red and hotter stars blue-white.
Wien's law: peak wavelength = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / T (m). Stefan-Boltzmann law: L = 4πR²σT⁴. The accretion-disk colours in the black-hole lab use the same blackbody physics.

Black holes

A black hole is mass compressed inside its Schwarzschild radius, r_s = 2GM/c². Inside that radius, the event horizon, not even light can escape. The black-hole lab renders one by tracing how light bends near it.

Key radii for a non-rotating hole: the photon sphere at 1.5 r_s (light can orbit), the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) at 3 r_s (the inner edge of the accretion disk), and the shadow radius 2.6 r_s. A clock hovering at radius r runs slow by √(1 − r_s/r).

Rotating black holes

Real black holes spin. A spinning (Kerr) black hole drags spacetime around with it: near it, everything is forced to turn. Its horizon shrinks, and a region called the ergosphere appears just outside, where nothing can stand still.

Spin a* = cJ/(GM²), from 0 to 1. Horizon r₊ = M(1 + √(1 − a²)). Orbits that move with the spin can come much closer: the prograde ISCO falls from 6M (a = 0) to 1M (a = 1), so gas releases up to 42% of its rest energy before falling in. Up to 29% of a maximally spinning hole's mass is rotational energy that could, in principle, be extracted (Penrose process).

Gravitational lensing
Mass bends the path of light. Stars behind a black hole appear shifted and stretched, and a star directly behind it becomes a ring of light: an Einstein ring.
Light passing a mass M at distance b is deflected by 4GM/(c²b), twice the Newtonian value. Eddington confirmed this in 1919. Einstein-ring angle: θ_E = √(4GM/c² × D_ls / (D_l D_s)).

Microlensing

When a dark object passes in front of a distant star, its gravity briefly brightens the star, by the same amount in every colour. Astronomers use this to find planets, lone black holes and other things that give off no light.

Magnification A = (u² + 2) / (u √(u² + 4)), where u is the lens-star separation in Einstein radii. The event lasts about one Einstein-radius crossing time, which grows with the square root of the lens mass.

Primordial black holes

Black holes made by dying stars weigh at least a few Suns. But in the first second after the Big Bang, dense pockets of the young universe could have collapsed into black holes of any mass, even the mass of a planet. None had been confirmed in 2025.

A planet-mass black hole would be tiny: six Earth masses fit inside r_s ≈ 5.3 cm. Some physicists have proposed that the hypothetical Planet Nine could be such an object (Scholtz & Unwin, 2020). Primordial black holes are also a dark-matter candidate.

Gravity
Mars' gravity is 3.72 m/s², 38% of Earth's. A jump that lifts you 20 cm on Earth lifts you about 54 cm on Mars, and falls take longer.
Jump height h = v²/2g. Hang time t = 2v/g. A suited astronaut with life support weighs about 200 kg, which is 745 N on Mars, about what a 76 kg person weighs on Earth.

Orbital mechanics
A spacecraft in orbit is falling around the planet. Higher orbits are slower and take longer. Mars' areostationary orbit, which matches the planet's spin, sits 17,030 km above the surface.

Circular speed v = √(μ/r); period T = 2π√(r³/μ). For Mars, μ = 4.2828 × 10¹³ m³/s² and the radius is 3,389.5 km. Near a black hole these Newtonian formulas fail: orbits precess, and inside the ISCO no stable orbit exists.

Time dilation

Clocks run slower in strong gravity. Near a black hole the effect becomes dramatic: an astronaut hovering just above the horizon would age far more slowly than friends far away. It isn't an illusion; both clocks are correct in their own place.

A static observer at radius r ticks at dτ/dt = √(1 − r_s/r) compared with a distant one. An orbiting observer is slowed further by its speed: for a circular orbit around a Schwarzschild hole, dτ/dt = √(1 − 3r_s/2r). The answer depends on how you move, which is why one comparison is never universal.

Tidal forces

Gravity pulls harder on the near side of an object than the far side. The difference stretches it toward the mass and squeezes it sideways. Near a small black hole tides are extreme; near a supermassive one you could cross the horizon without noticing.

The stretch across a length L at distance r is Δa ≈ 2GML/r³; the sideways squeeze is half of that. Because the horizon grows with M but tides fall with M/r³, tides at the horizon get weaker as black holes get heavier.

Motion
Newton's laws are the same on Mars, but lower gravity means less friction. Rovers need more distance to stop, and astronauts tend to lope instead of walking.
Walking speed is limited by the Froude number Fr = v²/(gL). Humans switch to running near Fr ≈ 0.5, so on Mars the walk-to-run transition happens near 1.3 m/s instead of 2.1 m/s.

Energy
Everything in the colony runs on energy budgets. One kilowatt-hour runs a 1,000 W heater for one hour. Solar panels make power only in daylight, so batteries carry the colony through the night.
Battery size needed: E = P_night × t_night / (depth of discharge × round-trip efficiency). A Mars night lasts about 12.3 hours at the equinox.

Thermodynamics
Mars is cold because it is far from the Sun and its thin atmosphere holds little heat. At Jezero crater the air swings from about −85 °C before dawn to about −10 °C in the afternoon.

Radiative equilibrium: T = [S(1 − A)/(4σ)]^¼. With S = 586 W/m² and albedo 0.25, T is about 210 K (−63 °C). The 0.6 kPa CO2 atmosphere adds only about 5 K of greenhouse warming, against about 33 K on Earth.

Electrolysis
An electric current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen: 2 H2O → 2 H2 + O2. Each kilogram of oxygen needs 1.125 kg of water.
Thermodynamic minimum: 39.4 kWh per kg H2 (higher heating value). Practical PEM cells need about 50 kWh/kg H2, or about 6.3 kWh per kg O2. The colony's oxygen plant can switch to this mode.

CO2 processing (MOXIE)
Mars' air is 95% carbon dioxide. Perseverance's MOXIE experiment heated CO2 to about 800 °C and split it: 2 CO2 → 2 CO + O2. Between 2021 and 2023 it made 122 g of oxygen, up to 12 g per hour.

MOXIE used about 300 W for about 6 g/h, about 50 kWh/kg including compressor and heaters. A scaled-up plant for a crewed ascent vehicle is estimated at about 25 kW for 2 kg/h, roughly 11 kWh/kg (Hecht et al., 2021).

Oxygen generation
A resting adult uses about 0.84 kg of oxygen per day. The colony makes oxygen in three ways: solid-oxide CO2 electrolysis, water electrolysis and photosynthesis in the greenhouse.
NASA's Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (NASA/TP-2015-218570) gives 0.82 kg O2 per crew member per day at nominal activity, rising during heavy outdoor work.

Chemical reactions
The Sabatier reaction turns CO2 and hydrogen into methane rocket fuel and water: CO2 + 4 H2 → CH4 + 2 H2O. It releases heat, and Mars has plenty of CO2.
Sabatier is exothermic (ΔH = −165 kJ/mol) and runs at 300-400 °C over a nickel or ruthenium catalyst. With electrolysis it closes the loop that makes methane and oxygen propellant on Mars.

Photosynthesis
Plants use light to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O → C6H12O6 + 6 O2. A greenhouse makes food and also recycles air.
Producing 1 kg of dry biomass releases roughly 1.07 kg of O2. About 20 to 50 m² of high-light crop area per person can supply most of one person's oxygen.

Plant growth
Under LEDs, lettuce is ready in about 6 weeks, wheat in 10 weeks and potatoes in 15 weeks. Light, water, nutrients, CO2 and temperature all set how fast plants grow.
Growth tracks the daily light integral (DLI, mol of photons per m² per day). Lettuce needs about 14-17 mol/m²/d. At 2.8 µmol/J LED efficacy, every 1 mol/m²/d costs about 0.1 kWh/m².

Hydroponics
Hydroponic crops grow in nutrient solution instead of soil. Martian regolith contains toxic perchlorates, so a colony grows food hydroponically at first.
A closed greenhouse condenses transpired water and reuses about 95% of it. Nutrient film technique (NFT) recirculates a thin film of solution past the roots, using far less water than field farming.

Ecosystems
A long-term colony needs a balanced loop: plants make oxygen and food, people make CO2 and waste, and microbes recycle the waste into nutrients.

Projects like Biosphere 2 and MELiSSA (ESA) showed how hard closed ecosystems are to balance: in Biosphere 2, soil microbes consumed oxygen faster than predicted. That is why the colony keeps machine life support as a backup.
Solar power
Sunlight on Mars is weaker than on Earth, and dust in the air and on the panels cuts it further. Mars Pathfinder's panels lost about 0.3% of their output every sol to settling dust.

Panel output = irradiance × area × efficiency × (1 − dust). Direct sunlight falls off as exp(−τ / cos z). The colony model fits Appelbaum and Flood's (1990) diffuse-light tables to within about 5% for τ from 0.5 to 5.

Life-support systems
Life support keeps the air breathable, the pressure safe and the temperature comfortable. It scrubs CO2, adds oxygen, removes humidity and recycles water.
Per crew member per day: 0.84 kg O2, about 1.0 kg CO2 removed, about 2.5 kg drinking water, about 1.8 kg food including packaging water (NASA BVAD). The ISS recovers about 98% of its water.

Water recycling
Water is too heavy to ship from Earth, so a colony recycles almost all of it: urine, humidity from the air and wash water are all purified and reused.
The ISS Water Recovery System uses vapour compression distillation for urine plus multifiltration and catalytic oxidation. It reached 98% recovery in 2023.

Spacecraft systems
A rocket's change in velocity (delta-v) depends on its engine efficiency and how much of its mass is propellant. Leaving Mars for low orbit takes about 4.1 km/s; leaving Earth takes about 9.4 km/s.
Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation: Δv = Isp × g0 × ln(m0 / m1). Methane and oxygen engines reach Isp of about 360-380 s in vacuum.

Martian gravity
Mars pulls with 3.72 m/s², 38% of Earth's gravity. You weigh less, jump higher and fall slower, but your bones and muscles weaken unless you exercise every day.
Atmospheric pressure
Mars' air presses at about 0.61 kPa, under 1% of Earth's. Below 6.3 kPa (the Armstrong limit) body fluids boil at body temperature, so every step outside needs a pressurised suit.
Astronaut life support

A suit supplies pure oxygen at 29.6 kPa, scrubs CO2, controls temperature and gives about eight hours outside. Habitats run near 70 kPa with a nitrogen-oxygen mix, so crews pre-breathe oxygen before going out.
Photovoltaic cells
A solar cell is a sandwich of semiconductors. A photon knocks an electron free and the junction drives it into a current. Triple-junction GaAs cells convert about 29% of sunlight to electricity.
Battery storage
ARES-1 stores daytime power in 400 kWh of lithium batteries kept warm inside containers. Draining them completely shortens their life, so the colony plans for 80% depth of discharge.
Solid-oxide electrolysis
At 800 °C a zirconia ceramic lets oxygen ions through but nothing else. Push CO2 past one side, apply a voltage, and pure oxygen comes out of the other: 2 CO2 → 2 CO + O2.
Martian atmosphere
95% carbon dioxide, 2.6% nitrogen, 1.9% argon and just 0.17% oxygen. It is too thin to breathe or to hold heat, but thick enough to carry dust storms that can circle the planet.
Water ice on Mars
Radar from orbit has mapped ice sheets buried under a metre or two of dust at mid-latitudes. Exposed ice sublimates in the thin air, but under cover it can survive for millions of years.
Filtration and distillation
Filters remove particles; distillation boils water away from dissolved salts and perchlorates and condenses it clean. Together they turn raw Martian ice into drinking water.
Photosynthesis and respiration
In light, plants turn CO2 and water into sugar and oxygen. Day and night they also respire, burning some sugar for energy. A crop grows only when photosynthesis outpaces respiration.
Controlled agriculture
Without soil, a farmer controls everything: nutrients, acidity, light, temperature, humidity and CO2. Done well, a square metre can produce many times what a field does.
Closed-loop life support

In a closed loop, waste from one process feeds another: people's CO2 feeds plants, plants' oxygen feeds people, and waste becomes fertiliser. Every percent recovered is cargo that never has to fly from Earth.
Colony governance

ARES-1 was built by the International Space Authority, but its council of colonists decides daily life. How far a settlement 20 light-minutes from Earth should govern itself is the defining question of 2189.
Gravitational microlensing

When an unseen mass drifts in front of a star, the star brightens for days and fades again, symmetric and identical in every colour. The event's length reveals the mass of something that emits no light at all.
Olympus Observatory
ARES-1's 2.4 m survey telescope in a 1,400 km orbit. Above the dust and with no air to blur its view, it measures two million stars every night for changes as small as 0.1%.
Radio astronomy
Radio telescopes collect signals far weaker than the noise around them. Narrowing the bandwidth cuts the noise; integrating longer lets the signal add up while random noise averages out.
PROJECT HORIZON

ISA deep-space mission, launched from Mars orbit in 2171 with four crew under Commander Ilse Varga, to study a lensing anomaly in the outer Solar System. Contact was lost in 2172. Official cause: reactor failure.
Kerr black holes
In 1963 Roy Kerr solved Einstein's equations for a spinning black hole. Its horizon shrinks with spin, an ergosphere forms outside it, and it drags spacetime around: frame dragging.
Light bending
General relativity predicts that light passing a mass M at distance b turns by 4GM/(c²b), twice Newton's value. The 1919 eclipse expedition measured it for the Sun and made Einstein famous.
Primordial black holes
Black holes that formed in the first second of the universe, not from dying stars. They can have any mass, even a planet's. HORIZON-1, six Earth masses in a 5 cm horizon, is the first ever found.
What happened to Horizon

Horizon's navigation assumed 0.6 Earth masses. The real object was ten times heavier, and its flyby flung the ship onto an escape path. Before they were lost, the crew placed three instrument pods in stable orbits and kept transmitting. They chose the data.
Dr. Chen's favourite stars
Betelgeuse, a red supergiant that will one day explode; Vega, spinning so fast it bulges at the equator; and Sirius B, a white dwarf the size of Earth with the mass of the Sun.
The ghost relay
An unregistered ISA satellite in a 20,000 km orbit, sending encrypted bursts through ARES-1's dish every night. Nobody at the colony knew it existed.
The Ares-0 expedition
The first crewed landing in Jezero, in 2161: four crew under Commander Tomas Halvorsen. Their greenhouse failed and their water ran short; three returned home, including a young Maya Reyes.
The end of Ares-0
With one ascent seat short, Halvorsen stayed behind with the survey data so the next crew would not start from nothing. His ice map made ARES-1 possible.
Minerals of Jezero
Hematite spherules and gypsum veins formed in water; unweathered olivine marks rock that stayed dry. Together they map where and how long the ancient lake lasted.
Marsquakes
NASA's InSight lander recorded over 1,300 marsquakes. The gap between fast P-waves and slower S-waves gives the distance; together they revealed Mars' liquid iron core.
Lava tubes
Tunnels left by flowing lava. Where a roof collapses, a skylight opens. Inside, temperatures barely change, radiation is a few percent of the surface, and ice can survive.
Phobos and Deimos
Mars' two small moons. Phobos rises in the west and sets in the east twice a day and is slowly falling toward Mars; Deimos drifts across the sky over two and a half days.
Measuring gravity
A pendulum's period depends only on its length and on gravity: T = 2π√(L/g). With a string and a stopwatch you can weigh a planet.
Martian dust
Martian dust is finer than talc and slightly magnetic. It settles on panels at about 0.3% of their output per sol and gets into every seal and bearing.
Orbital precession

In general relativity an orbit doesn't quite close: the ellipse turns a little every lap. Mercury's orbit turns 43 arcseconds per century more than Newton predicts, one of the first tests Einstein passed.
Binary stars
About half of all stars have a companion. Kepler's third law turns their orbit into a mass: M = a³/P² in solar masses, AU and years.
Near-Earth asteroids
Radar measures an asteroid's distance from the echo delay, d = ct/2, to within metres. Planetary defence depends on knowing these orbits years ahead.
Neutron stars
The crushed core of a massive star: more mass than the Sun in a ball 12 km across. Pulsars sweep radio beams across space like lighthouses, some hundreds of times a second.
Einstein rings
When a source lies exactly behind a lens, its light arrives from every side at once and spreads into a ring. Telescopes have photographed dozens around distant galaxies.
Accretion disks
Gas falling into a black hole spirals inward, heats by friction to millions of kelvin and glows. Near the hole, Doppler beaming makes the approaching side brighter and gravity reddens the light.
Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
Launched in 2005, its HiRISE camera photographed Mars in metre-scale detail for decades. Its archive still holds images no human has looked at.
Commander Maya Reyes

ARES-1's commander, 52. The youngest member of the Ares-0 crew in 2161 and one of the three who flew home when Commander Halvorsen gave up his seat. Calm, protective, and stubborn about bringing everyone back.
Dr. Elias Chen
Chief astrophysicist. Came to Mars for the darkest sky humans have ever had, and stayed for the questions it raised. Reads observatory data over breakfast and forgets to eat.
Engineer Nara Erdene
Life-support engineer from Arkhangai, Mongolia. Grew up among herders who wasted nothing; runs ARES-1's air and water the same way. Doesn't hand out compliments, and means every one she gives.
Dr. Amara Okafor
Chief botanist from Lagos. Her first garden was a window box; now she runs the only farm on a planet. Breeds wheat for low gravity and argues with Nara about water every day.
Jun Park
Communications engineer. Keeps the dish, the satellites and every message home running. Listens to the noise between stars at night, which is how he found what everyone else missed.
Rafael Ortiz
Chief mechanic. Fixed tractors in Sonora before fixing everything on Mars. Names every machine, and believes they work better for it.
Dr. Lena Sorensen
Medical officer. Treats radiation, bone loss and loneliness, and believes the last is the most dangerous. Checks every colonist after every storm, without exception.
Commander Ilse Varga
PROJECT HORIZON's commander, a classmate of Maya Reyes and by every account the best of their class. Led her crew of four to the edge of the Solar System in 2171.
Commander Tomas Halvorsen
Commander of Ares-0, the first crew in Jezero. Stayed behind in 2163 so his crew could launch home. His survey of the ice made ARES-1 possible.
